Differentiate each coordinate, then combine the three components.
**Step 1 — differentiate.**
x = a cos ωt → v_x = **−aω sin ωt**
y = a sin ωt → v_y = **+aω cos ωt**
z = aωt → v_z = **aω**
**Step 2 — form the speed.**
v = √(v_x² + v_y² + v_z²)
= √(a²ω² sin²ωt + a²ω² cos²ωt + a²ω²)
**Step 3 — use sin² + cos² = 1.**
v = √(a²ω² + a²ω²)
= √(2a²ω²)
= **√2 aω** ✓
**What the motion looks like.** The x and y coordinates trace a **circle** of radius a in
the horizontal plane, while z rises steadily ✓ The particle therefore moves along a
**helix**, like a point on a screw thread - the standard path of a charged particle in a
uniform magnetic field.
**Why the speed is constant.** The time-dependent terms cancel through the Pythagorean
identity ✓ The particle travels its helix at an unvarying √2 aω, even though its
**velocity** is turning continuously.
**The two contributions.**
circular part: speed **aω** - the familiar v = ωr
axial part: speed **aω** as well, since dz/dt = aω ✓
They are perpendicular, so they combine as √(a²ω² + a²ω²) = √2 aω, not by addition.
**The pitch of the helix.** In one revolution, taking T = 2π/ω, the particle rises
z = aω(2π/ω) = **2πa** ✓ equal to the circumference of the circle - which is why the two
speed components come out equal and the answer carries a √2.
**A numerical check.** Take a = 1 m and ω = 1 rad s⁻¹, at t = 0:
v̄ = (0, 1, 1), so v = √2 = **1·41 m s⁻¹**
at t = π/2: v̄ = (−1, 0, 1), again √2 ✓ unchanged, as the algebra promised.
**Reading the distractors.** **aω** ✗ is the circular part alone, ignoring the rise.
**2aω** ✗ adds the two components arithmetically instead of in quadrature. **√3 aω** ✗
would need three equal perpendicular components, but there are only two ✓
∴ √2 aω.

Turn the velocity components into dy/dx and integrate - the time drops out.
**Step 1 — read off the components.** From v̄ = K(y î + x ĵ):
dx/dt = **Ky**
dy/dt = **Kx**
**Step 2 — divide one by the other.** The constant K and the time both cancel:
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)
= Kx/Ky
= **x/y**
**Step 3 — separate and integrate.**
y dy = x dx
y²/2 = x²/2 + c
**y² = x² + constant** ✓
**What the path looks like.** y² − x² = constant is a **rectangular hyperbola** with
asymptotes y = ±x ✓ The particle sweeps along one branch of it.
**Why eliminating t is the right move.** The question asks for the **path**, a relation
between x and y alone ✓ Solving for x(t) and y(t) separately would work but is longer:
it gives x = A e^(Kt) + B e^(−Kt) and similar for y, from which the same hyperbola
follows.
**A check on a particular solution.** Take x = cosh(Kt), y = sinh(Kt):
dx/dt = K sinh(Kt) = **Ky** ✓
dy/dt = K cosh(Kt) = **Kx** ✓ both equations satisfied
and x² − y² = cosh² − sinh² = **1**, a constant ✓ exactly the predicted form.
**The special case through the origin.** If the constant is zero, y² = x² gives
**y = ±x** - the straight-line asymptotes themselves ✓ A particle starting on one of
those lines stays on it for ever.
**Reading the distractors.** **xy = constant** ✗ is the path for v̄ = K(y î − x ĵ) or
similar, giving dy/dx = −y/x. **y² = x + constant** ✗ and **y = x² + constant** ✗ are
parabolas; integrating y dy = x dx cannot produce a first power on one side and a square
on the other ✓ The symmetry of the velocity in x and y guarantees that the answer must
be symmetric in x and y too, which only y² = x² + constant is.
∴ y² = x² + constant.

The acceleration is entirely in y, so the x motion is **uniform** - and that is what ties
the parabola to a particular v_x.
**Step 1 — write each coordinate as a function of time.** The particle starts at the
origin at t = 0.
in x: no acceleration, so **x = v_x t**
in y: constant acceleration a from rest in that direction, so **y = ½at²**
**Step 2 — substitute into the given path.**
y = bx²
½at² = b(v_x t)²
½at² = b v_x² t²
**Step 3 — cancel t² and solve.**
½a = b v_x²
v_x² = a/(2b)
**v_x = √[a/(2b)]** ✓
**Why v_x must be constant.** The acceleration has **no x component**, so by Newton's
first law the x velocity never changes ✓ That is what allows x = v_x t with no ½at² term,
and it is the key step.
**Why the answer is a single fixed number.** The path y = bx² is a specific parabola. A
particle with a different v_x would trace a different parabola under the same
acceleration ✓ So the geometry of the path **determines** the horizontal speed.
**A numerical instance.** Take a = 8 m s⁻² and b = 1 m⁻¹:
v_x = √(8/2) = **2 m s⁻¹**
check at t = 1 s: x = 2 m, y = ½(8)(1) = 4 m, and bx² = 1(4) = **4 m** ✓ the point lies
on the parabola, as required.
**The projectile parallel.** This is exactly the structure of projectile motion, with
y = ½gt² playing the part of the fall and x = v_x t the horizontal drift ✓ There too the
trajectory is a parabola whose shape is fixed by the launch speed.
**A check on the dimensions.** b has units of 1/length (since bx² must be a length), so
a/b has units of (length/time²) x length = (length/time)², and its square root is a
**speed** ✓ The option √(2b/a) would be the reciprocal of a speed, and √(ba) has the
wrong units too - a dimensional check eliminates several options at once.
**Reading the distractors.** **√(2b/a)** ✗ inverts the ratio. **√(a/b)** ✗ loses the
factor 2 that comes from ½at². **√(b/a)** ✗ and **√(ba)** ✗ fail on dimensions ✓
∴ √[a/(2b)].
